Thanks, this was exactly right and I should have caught it. The path was registered absolute but only credited when `_PATH_TOKEN` yielded it as one token, so any clone location with a space, a parenthesis, or a drive-letter colon split it and the reviewer could never earn credit even after reading the exact file. That turns the guard into a wall nobody can pass, on tasks that used to reach a verdict. Fixed in 47fc2c5.

**The fix, as you suggested.** `note_event` now also matches each whole tool-input string leaf (backslashes normalized to forward slashes) against the required paths with the same `_names_path` rule, alongside the tokens. A `Read` of the exact file is credited wherever the repo lives, and a path that already matched is unchanged. Your four cases now all credit:

```
/home/u/lib/src/a.py          -> credited
/home/u/My Lib/src/a.py       -> credited
/home/u/lib (copy)/src/a.py   -> credited
C:/Users/u/lib/src/a.py       -> credited
```

**Tests.** The clone-location cases are added as a parametrized tracker test plus a Windows-backslash-spelling test, all running on every platform. With the exact read now credited everywhere, I dropped the `skipif` on the referenced-stands integration test and it passes on Windows too.

**Docstring.** Reworded the `InspectionTracker` scope note to describe the whole-leaf match, so it matches the code rather than only the token path.

I would like to take this. It is the same area as my earlier exec_names work (#320 / the host-independent fold tests), so let me lay out the approach before a PR, since it touches the frozen `guard.py`.

**Diagnosis on current `main`:** #339 landed the measurement, but every guard call site still resolves the case fold from the process, not the command. `command_name(argv[0], is_windows=_IS_WINDOWS)` is called with no `cwd`/`fold_case`, so it falls to `host_folds_case()` with no arguments, which probes this process's `os.getcwd()` + `PATH` (and the `sys.executable`/tempdir fallbacks), never the worktree that `evaluate(cwd=...)` documents as "where the backend will actually run the command." On a mixed-volume install the two disagree and the process-case-sensitive / worktree-case-insensitive pairing fails open, exactly as your table shows.

**Two halves, matching your table:**

1. **argv side** (`GH pr merge 7`): thread the command's `cwd` into the fold decision. Compute the fold once from `host_folds_case(cwd)` in `evaluate()`/`denial_reason()` and pass it as `fold_case=` to the `command_name(...)` calls (they already accept it, and it is cached on `(cwd, path_env)` so repeated calls are cheap). This closes the argv cells without changing any POSIX/case-sensitive-CI verdict.

2. **raw-text side** (`RM -rf /`, `GIT push origin main`): these decide through the import-time-compiled matchers (`_RM_RF`, `_GIT_DESTRUCTIVE`, `_FORGE_MERGE`, ...) whose `case_flags()` is fixed at import with no `cwd`. `exec_names.case_flags`'s own docstring already calls this the documented residual. To close it, the destructive/merge raw-text checks in `evaluate()` (where `cwd` is known) would re-match with the fold taken from `host_folds_case(cwd)` rather than trusting the import-time flag. I would keep the matcher patterns as-is and apply the case flag at match time keyed on the command's `cwd`, which is the design-worthy part you flagged.

I lean to your option that folds when either the module/process anchor or the worktree folds, so the result is fail-closed and immune to the pairing question.

**Frozen-file note:** `guard.py` is at its 3036-line budget, so I will keep any new logic in `exec_names.py` and edit the guard call sites in place, and pin the property with a parametrised test (fold in / fold out) so it stays checkable from either kind of host rather than depending on the CI machine.

Does that direction (thread `cwd`; re-match raw text with the cwd fold; fold-if-either) sound right to you before I open the PR? Happy to split it into the argv half first if you would prefer to land it in two steps.

I looked into this. The root cause is in `item()` (`tomlkit/items.py`): it early-returns an already-parsed `Table`/`InlineTable`/`AoT` unchanged, so under `sort_keys` only the top-level container (which reaches the dict-rebuild branch) is sorted, while nested items keep their original order.

Ran the `test_git_quoted_paths.py` subset on a real Windows 11 host (26200, cp1252) and traced the seven failures. Two distinct causes, both in the test harness rather than the shipped code:

1. `_git` and `_committed_names` decode git output with a bare `text=True`, i.e. the host codepage. Git reports paths as UTF-8, so the accented name comes back mojibake and the two committed-name assertions fail. Production is not affected: `GitRepo._run`/`_run_null` already force `encoding="utf-8"`. The `résumé.txt` and `données` cases pass on Windows precisely because they run through the production path, not through the helper.

2. The `"`, `\` and TAB parametrized cases cannot run on Windows at all. Those characters are the ones Win32 forbids in a filename, so `Path.write_text` raises `OSError 22` before the guard is reached. They exercise git's unconditional C-quoting, which no legal Windows filename can trigger.

#560 fixes the first (the helpers now decode UTF-8, mirroring production) and skips the second on Windows only, leaving POSIX byte-for-byte unchanged: 6 passed and 5 skipped on Windows, all 11 still run on POSIX. It is scoped to this one file, and it does not touch the `test_git_config_exec.py` six you de-escalated above, the `ls-remote` latency budget, or the Windows CI job's file list.

Now that the environment mix-up is sorted (my checkout had CLDR 47 while master expects 48.2), this is a small, self-contained CLDR-compliance fix. `format_compact_decimal` picks the magnitude from the unrounded value and only rounds afterward, so a rounding carry keeps the smaller unit and emits compact forms that are not valid: `999999` renders as `'1000K'` (should be `1M`), `999999999` as `'1000M'` (should be `1B`), and `-999999` as `'-1000K'`. Per CLDR UTS #35, which the function's own docstring links, the pattern is selected from the rounded value.

Agreed, that is the right call, and it is the faithful inverse of `format()` (`{:#x}` always emits the prefix, `{:x}` never does), so parsing should mirror that. I have pushed a commit that implements exactly your matrix:

```python
parse("{:x}",  "0xff") is None
parse("{:#x}", "0xff") == 255
parse("{:x}",  "ff")   == 255
parse("{:#x}", "ff")   is None
```

## One signal, three consumers

A new `agent/fs_case.py` — sibling to `fs_roots.py` and `exec_names.py`, so `guard.py` gains no lines:

```python
def is_case_insensitive_fs(path: str) -> bool:
    """Whether `path`'s filesystem case-folds. Probed once, cached per process."""
```

Honoring your two requirements exactly:

- **Cached per process, not per call.** Module-level `functools.lru_cache` (or a plain module global) keyed on the mount, so `evaluate()` adds no syscall after the first. The probe itself is one `os.path.exists` on an upper/lower variant of a known file, or the `stat`-two-spellings trick your `cp` output shows — done once.
- **Flippable in tests.** The three consumers take the result as a parameter, exactly as `fs_roots.is_windows_filesystem_root(is_windows=...)` and `exec_names.command_name(is_windows=...)` do, so CI exercises both readings from one host. `evaluate()` resolves the real value once and threads it down; tests pass their own. That is the property whose absence let this gap survive, so it is non-negotiable in the fix.

## What it feeds

1. **`exec_names.command_name`** — the fold decision changes from `is_windows` to `case_insensitive`. On macOS (case-insensitive, not Windows) `GH` now folds to `gh`; on Linux CI it does not. Both docstrings become true at once, which is your framing.
2. **The raw-text matchers** (#305's open half): `_RM_RF`, `_FORGE_*`, `_GIT_WRITE`, `_LEXICAL_MERGE_STACK`, `_LEXICAL_LIVE_SERVER`. These are where `RM -rf /` and `gh.exe`/`.cmd` in text still slip. Compiling them `re.IGNORECASE` **when the fs is case-insensitive** closes the casing cells; a shared suffix fragment (not inline per-site — your #307 note) closes the `.exe` cells.
3. Nothing else — I will enumerate the matcher set **by script**, not by eye, precisely because #307 missed `_LEXICAL_MERGE_STACK` and `_LEXICAL_LIVE_SERVER` doing it by hand. The script's output goes in the PR so the set is auditable.

## Scope and caveats I want on the record before starting

- **`RM -rf /` is open on Windows too**, not only macOS — I measured that on #328 already. So the raw-text casing fix is not macOS-only; on a case-insensitive host of either kind these fold. The probe is the right gate for all of it.

- This is a behaviour change on **every** platform for the raw-text half (more denials), so I will run the same false-denial corpus I used on #331 (135 commands × wrappers, diffed both readings) and put the numbers in the body.

If a cell stays open at the end it gets an asserting test like the raw-text one, and it is `Refs`, not `Closes`, until the matrix is green on both readings.

```
_IS_WINDOWS=False (Mac/dogfood):
  GH pr merge 7                      ALLOW    (gh   -> DENY)
  RM -rf /                           ALLOW    (rm   -> DENY)
  FIND / -delete                     ALLOW    (find -> DENY)
  sh -c "GIT.CMD push origin main"   ALLOW    (git  -> DENY)

```

`NH approve 7` denies even unfolded, because `_approve_denial` also consults a case-insensitive `_GATE_MENTION`. So constraint #2 survives the casing gap — which narrows the severity from what the title implies, and is worth stating so the fix is not scoped as "the agent can merge."

**2. `RM -rf /` is allowed on Windows too, not only on the Mac reading:**

```
_IS_WINDOWS=True:
  RM -rf /        ALLOW      <- still open, even where my fold applies
  GH pr merge 7   DENY
  FIND / -delete  DENY
```

That is the load-bearing subtlety for whichever fix lands: `GH`/`FIND` go through `exec_names` (argv-based), so my Windows fold already catches them. **`RM -rf /` does not** — `_RM_RF` is a raw-text regex that never sees a basename, so folding the name resolver cannot reach it. A complete casing fix has to make the **raw-text matchers** (`_RM_RF`, and the `find`/`rg`/`grep` scan patterns if they are literal too) case-insensitive on a case-insensitive host, not just the argv path.

**On the resolution:** your "fold when the filesystem is measurably case-insensitive" is the right call, and better than my `is_windows` proxy — macOS is the case it misses, and it is exactly your dogfood host. One probe cached per process, replacing an assumption with a measurement, is the same shape as taking `is_windows` as a parameter rather than reading `os.name`. It just needs to feed both the `exec_names` fold **and** the raw-text matchers.

## `Closes` was over-claiming, and is now `Refs`

Every row you measured reproduces here. Three of them survive any name resolver, because they decide through **raw-text matchers** rather than argv[0]:

```
rm.exe -rf /                    _RM_RF matches text, not a basename
echo "gh.exe pr merge 7" | sh   lexical merge-stack matcher
```

So the cheat sheet remains reachable only by navigating to About and clicking a button.

## 3. The opening card is a dialog that never takes focus

`Complete AI configuration` is not just a card:

```
role="dialog"   aria-label="Complete AI configuration"
aria-modal      null
position        relative,  z-index auto
document.activeElement on load   BODY
```

So it is announced to assistive technology as a dialog, it is not modal, and focus never moves to it. It sits at position 8 of 23 in the tab order, in the sidebar. A sighted user reads it as a notice card, which is what it looks like, and the role says something stronger.

## 4. Escape closes the drawer but not that dialog

The cheat sheet lists `Esc` as "Close dialog or drawer" with `when: "always"`, and `shortcuts.js` says every dialog closes itself via `useEscapeKey`. Measured:

```
Escape on the task drawer            closes it
Escape on the opening dialog         does nothing
```

Both carry `role="dialog"`. The documented behaviour holds for one and not the other, and the one it does not hold for is the one a new user meets first.

## 5. The task drawer leads with a 32 character hex id

Opening `Add mul() to calc` renders, in order:

```
75e5a95fe9044b2f85a4d3c924e7c5b5
Add mul() to calc — ready for you
```

The identifier is above the title, in the position the eye lands on first. It is the least useful string in the drawer for a human, and the title, which is the useful one, is second.

## 6. A minor one, and I am less sure it matters

While the drawer slides in, it renders partly transparent over the board for a few hundred milliseconds, and during that window both layers are readable at once and neither is legible. It resolves as soon as the animation finishes. On a fast machine you would probably never notice; I only saw it because a screenshot caught it mid transition.

## What I would take from this list

Items 1 and 4 are the two I would fix, and both are small. Item 1 needs a decision about wording rather than code, since the fix is to say what each number counts. Item 4 looks like the opening card simply not using `useEscapeKey` like the other dialogs do.

Items 3 and 5 are judgement calls that are yours, not mine.

Everything below is from `aider-chat` **0.86.2** in a clean `ubuntu:24.04` container. **No API key was used**, and none was needed: every question here is answered from package metadata, from argparse, or from behaviour that fails before any request is made. So the smoke-provenance question I asked you is not blocking this half, and I did not wait on it.

## Terms

`aider-chat` is **Apache 2.0** (`License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License`, from installed package metadata).

Worth separating, because `INTEGRATIONS_LEGAL.md` is about more than the licence: Aider is bring-your-own-key, so it makes no vendor relationship of its own. The terms that bind a run are the **model provider's**, reached with the operator's own credential, exactly as with Codex. Nothing in Aider's own licensing restricts driving it programmatically.

## It can be driven headlessly

`--message` / `--message-file` with `--yes-always` work, and the hygiene flags an adapter needs are all present:

```
--message  --message-file  --yes-always  --exit  --dry-run
--no-pretty  --no-stream  --no-git  --no-auto-commits  --no-analytics
--model  --weak-model  --map-tokens  --show-diffs  --verbose
--lint  --test  --auto-test  --restore-chat-history  --load
```

A correction to my own claim: the flag is `--yes-always`, not `--yes`.

**A methodological note, because my first pass was wrong.** I initially grepped `--help` text and reported `--no-pretty`, `--no-stream`, `--no-git`, `--no-auto-commits` and `--verbose` as ABSENT. They all exist. Argparse renders paired flags as `[--pretty | --no-pretty]`, which my regex missed. The list above comes from invoking each flag and checking whether argparse says `unrecognized arguments`, which is the difference between reading a name and following what it resolves to.

## Two findings that shape the adapter

### 1. The exit code carries no signal

This is the one I would want you to see before anything else.

| case | rc | elapsed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bogus key, with `--exit` | **0** | 5s |
| bogus key, without `--exit` | **0** | 4s |
| bogus key, adapter flags, no `--exit` | **0** | 4s |
| control: `--model no-such-model-xyz`, no auth involved | **0** | 4s |

`litellm.AuthenticationError: Incorrect API key provided` is printed, legibly, and the process still exits **0**. An unknown model does the same.

I isolated `--exit` deliberately: probe 2 measured `rc=0` while also passing `--exit`, which means "do startup then exit", so that could have been the cause. It was not.

What I have NOT shown: whether a *successful* run also exits 0. That needs a real key, which is the provenance question. So the precise claim is "every failure mode I could reach returns 0", not "the exit code is constant".

**Consequence:** an adapter cannot use the exit status to decide whether an attempt failed. It has to parse output, which is exactly the kind of fragile seam `BackendCapabilities` exists to make visible rather than bury.

### 2. With no model and no key it blocks on a browser

```
No LLM model was specified and no API keys were provided.
Please open this URL in your browser to connect Aider with OpenRouter:
https://openrouter.ai/auth?callback_url=http://localhost:8484/callback/aider&...
Waiting up to 5 minutes for you to finish in the browser...
```

`rc=124` at my 90-second kill, with `--message --yes-always` set. Unattended, that is a five-minute hang per attempt.

**Mitigable, and I checked rather than assumed:** it only happens when no model and no key are given. With an explicit `--model` and any key, even an invalid one, it fails in 4 seconds instead. An adapter that always passes both never enters that path.

## What the capability record would say

```python

    name="aider",
    blocks_tool_calls=False,      # no PreToolUse veto exists to wire
    post_tool_hooks=False,        # no per-tool-call callback
    session_resume=False,         # --restore-chat-history/--load are a history
```

`thinking_budget=True` is the only one I would declare True, and I would rather you sanity-check it than take my word: the flag exists and takes a value, but I have not watched it bite.

## Where that leaves it, and what I would like from you

Nothing here disqualifies Aider. The licence is clean, it drives headlessly, and the browser hang is avoidable. But the capability record is honest about being thin, and the exit-code finding means the adapter's failure detection is output parsing rather than a status check.
